📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

In a recent development, if you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the firm is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):.

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. I've spent the last week testing and reviewing the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited controller and the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset, and I highly recommend these for PS5 gamers. But of course, they're brand fresh and the controller especially isn't the cheapest.

Recent findings suggest that I think all PS5 players can agree that the first-party DualSense is, without a doubt, the best controller for the console. That's thanks to its haptic feedback and adaptive triggers that make play feel immersive — but the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is the PS5 controller for those who value precision above all else.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest advantages is the R5U's customizable layout as it's got four buttons on the back and two on the top, so you can assign frequently used actions to them without moving your thumbs from the sticks. I've found these particularly helpful during cop pursuits and fast-paced missions. Using the rear buttons to, say, accelerate and brake my car feels more natural, too.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of TMR sensors in the R5U's thumbsticks can't be overstated either. They're designed to reduce the traditional stick-drift issues that often plague conventional analog sticks, and they provide long-term reliability especially for players who plan on spending 200 hours in GTA 6.

When it comes to combat and cop chases, the Pulse makes gunfire, explosions and footsteps sound life-like. I've been thoroughly enjoying using the Pulse to play GTA 6, and I don't see that changing anytime soon.

After releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the firm is now rolling out the public beta for people looking to try the fresh features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with latest privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several new features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Industry observers note that and speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing fresh tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful upgrade, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and customers on the public beta can now try out these new features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

#96910. Tech Report: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2361 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Linebender ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linebender

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago.
  • The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong.
  • Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits unveiled since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

Industry observers note that for these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the notable quality criteria.

Sources indicate that I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance complications (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

In a recent development, while desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" blueprint for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

Industry observers note that that said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

Sources indicate that one of the major unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of upcoming Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This problem is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

According to recent reports, this is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

Sources indicate that one of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and patch the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

It has been revealed that for this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

Industry observers note that this philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

Industry observers note that that said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

According to recent reports, the Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

In a recent development, one good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Sources indicate that given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating upcoming layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

According to recent reports, for a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scott Wu, co-founder and chief executive of Cognition.

Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, is in talks to raise money at a $75bn valuation, two months after its last round. Bloomberg’s Rebecca Torrence reported the talks on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

Sources indicate that the tech giant is weighing a raise of $2bn or more, according to Bloomberg. The talks are ongoing and the details could change. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Recent findings suggest that most of the interest has come from current backers, Bloomberg reported. Avenir, Accel, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Lux Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners are in talks to take part, some of the people mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that avenir, Accel and Lux declined to comment to Bloomberg. Bessemer, Lightspeed and Cognition did not respond to its requests.

A completed deal would be Cognition’s third round this year. It has already raised more than $3bn in 2026, including over $2bn at a $48bn valuation in September. That round nearly doubled its value in 15 weeks, after a $26bn round in May.

The figure sits inside the range reported last month. In October, Business Insider’s Katie Roof reported investor offers valuing Cognition at $70bn to $80bn.

Investors have poured money into startups building AI agents for software work. Devin competes with Cursor, which SpaceX bought for $60bn. Days after that deal closed, SpaceX reportedly approached Cognition about a takeover too.

According to recent reports, cognition sells to companies including Citigroup and Nvidia. In September it mentioned it was on track for $1bn in annualised revenue, roughly double its run rate four months earlier. This month it signed an alliance with McKinsey to sell Devin to large firms.

Industry observers note that the size of the raises has drawn criticism. Ed Zitron, a critic of the AI industry’s spending, questioned the round on X.

“Why does this manufacturer need $5bn in the space of a year,” Zitron wrote.

Breaking: These 14 Newly introduced Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov.
  • It has been revealed that technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program.
  • The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the organization's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this upgrade isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially debuts the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

It has been revealed that technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger complications. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the organization's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a upcoming setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Presently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the major screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a newly introduced set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally revealed with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,.

According to recent reports, the tech giant generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these latest Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company notes Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Sources indicate that despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing upcoming abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

Industry observers note that for example, you could ask Siri AI to help you initiative a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These upcoming actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Sources indicate that continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these prepares to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

In a recent development, apple is also testing a upcoming Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

According to recent reports, another upcoming Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

According to recent reports, apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

It has been revealed that "Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

According to recent reports, if you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.).

Sources indicate that you can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

That’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller users. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

It has been revealed that adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

It has been revealed that the Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Sources indicate that both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

According to recent reports, A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller customers also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

The LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

Sources indicate that liberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

It has been revealed that for a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

There are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Recent findings suggest that omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

LiberNovo’s warranty covers the frame and structural components for six years, and electronic components for two years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks.
  • In a recent development, databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
  • The talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive of Databricks.

In a recent development, databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225bn, The Wall Street Journal’s Meghan Bobrowsky and Kate Clark reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. That would be nearly 20% above the $190bn valuation the data firm reached in August.

The talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, according to the Journal. TNW has not independently verified the report.

The latest money would come while Databricks stays private. Its chief executive, Ali Ghodsi, explained why in a recent interview on the All-In podcast.

Industry observers note that “We will go public. We are going to be public, but right now I think during this transition period of AI there’s just too much up and down, and I think it’s distracting to companies,” Ghodsi told All-In.

Databricks closed a $5bn round at $190bn in August. It mentioned then that it had passed a $7bn revenue run rate, the Journal reported.

Ghodsi told All-In the business is growing 70% to 80% a year, and that he wants more. He would like growth of 100%, “way over 100”, he remarked.

According to recent reports, the organization has added AI products this year. They include an agent called Genie One, which answers questions from a company’s business data, and Unity Gateway, which gives customers access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Genie also reached Slack this month, in a version that answers data questions inside the chat app.

It has been revealed that its investors include Coatue Management, Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Insight Partners, Fidelity and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, according to the Journal.

In a recent development, the Journal calls Databricks a candidate for a near-term listing. Investors say a strong showing by Anthropic, whose stock ended its first week worth $1.6tn, could unleash a wave of AI listings, the paper reported.

According to recent reports, ghodsi weighed both sides on All-In. A listing brings access to capital and a quarterly marketing moment, he stated. Staying private means Databricks must arrange its own tender offers for staff every year. He said employees have never used up all the money set aside for them.

In a recent development, his worry is volatility. When a stock falls, he noted, staff effectively take a pay cut, and some leave before the price recovers.

Ghodsi also said he believes AI has already reached artificial general intelligence, by the definition his Berkeley lab used around 2010. He put the risk of AI wiping out humanity close to zero, and named cyberattacks as the real danger.

“I think the cyber risk is real and really bad things can happen with that,” he said.

Our Saatva Classic Mattress review: ★★★★★User score: ★★★★★ (5,000+ reviews).

Recent findings suggest that still not sure if either of these would be the right cooling mattress for you? The Tom’s Guide Sleep Team has spent over 24,000 hours testing over 170 mattresses, and we’re sharing our top three shopping tips for hot sleepers here.

You may be tackling your hot sleeping issue by investing in a specialist cooling mattress, but it’s equally important to make sure the bed supports your sleep style and body weight (no back pain here, thank you.).

It has been revealed that generally, side sleepers benefit from beds on the softer end of the mattress firmness scale as more cushioning ensures their joints are cradled to avoid aches. Meanwhile, front and back sleepers need a firmer sleep surface to keep their hips aligned through the night, preventing back pain.

Body weight comes into it too. Firmer beds best support heavier bodies while lighter bodies would find these too harsh, needing a softer surface to sink into.

In fact, that’s another advantage when it comes to choosing to the Bear Elite Hybrid and Saatva Classic Mattresses — they both come in three firmness levels, from soft to medium and firm, to suit different bodies.

Industry observers note that other factors, like mobility and overnight manufacturer, can influence your mattress buying choices, too. People with reduced mobility may need a mattress with strong, sturdy edges they can push off from to get out of bed. Moreover, if you share a bed with a fidgety partner, you’ll want it to be good at absorbing motion so you can’t feel their movements from one side of the bed to the other.

In a recent development, A lot of mattresses these days come with some form of cooling properties, so knowing your firmness, comfort, and support preferences can narrow down your search — with best prices swarming the whole market around Black Friday mattress shopping can be a minefield. The last thing you want is to tackle one sleep problem but trigger another.

In a recent development, you can invest in the coolest mattress on the market, but dress it incorrectly and it’s game over. For maximum cooling, look for a breathable mattress protector and moisture-wicking bedsheets that will accentuate heat dissipation rather than trap warmth.

Industry observers note that according to our bedding experts, the Brooklyn Bedding Luxury Cooling Mattress Protector ($90.30 for a queen, down from $129 at Brooklyn Bedding now) is the best option for hot sleepers. This cool-to-touch protector kept our tester at a comfortable temperature through summer heatwaves, even in a home without air conditioning, while safeguarding their mattress from spills and stains.

Industry observers note that in terms of sheets, the Sijo Airyweight Eucalyptus Sheet Set is our top pick for warm bodies. Made with Tencel fabric, these sheets absorb moisture while staying lightweight so you don’t wake up sweaty or clammy.

Hybrid mattress are generally cooler than memory foam mattresses, no matter how much cooling gel is infused in their foams. Hybrid mattresses, which feature pocketed coil layers alongside layers of foam and other materials, allow better air circulation as heat can escape out of the bottom and sides of the bed rather than pooling beneath you.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, foam layers tend to act like sponges, holding on to any heat your body gives off as you sleep. Yes, cooling infusions (like Phase Change Material, GlacioTex and copper) can help manage that heat to some extent. But, ultimately, hybrid beds will always be more breathable and reliably temperature neutral.

Industry observers note that so, you're probably wondering which hybrid mattress we recommend to hot sleepers. In summary, the Bear Elite is a solid choice for chronic overheaters and the Saatva Classic is a great all-rounder for warm sleepers (especially those with back pain). But if you want knockout value, consider the Brooklyn Bedding Copperflex Pro Hybrid Mattress – just $932 for a queen in current Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales, this is a well built bed that sleeps impressively cool for its price point.

Also, let’s get this clear: cooling tends to mean temperature neutral, not actively refrigerating. Non-smart cooling mattresses generally use materials to help dissipate body heat rather than making the bed surface physically cold.

In a recent development, that noted, a smart air-or-water-based cooling mattress or mattress cover like the Eight Sleep Pod with automatic, responsive temperature controls can actively cool down your bed surface and adjust its temperature through the night in response to your fluctuations. And yes, it is as good as it sounds. If you’re seriously struggling with night sweats or hot flashes, and have a $2,600+ budget, we recommend investing.

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp owners: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the latest limit is rolling out to users on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”.

WhatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the upcoming limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the revision becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

Sources indicate that this rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the company confirmed four new features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

  • Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.
  • Sources indicate that samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.

Sources indicate that samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The firm announced the changes on Friday in Korea.

Sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung said in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.

In a recent development, samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung said it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly intends to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.

Sources indicate that sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.

In a recent development, choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the introduces of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.

It has been revealed that earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under fresh rules, the FT reported.

It has been revealed that the rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.

Samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.

It has been revealed that chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba noted this week the rules will slow growth in AI.

Industry observers note that some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.

In a recent development, samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement indicates it wants the upcoming team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

#96895. Split Radiance Cascades

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2652 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jacktollenaar ↗ Open Full Page

Split Radiance Cascades

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jacktollenaar

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, radiance cascades is a technique that massively improves global illumination without much extra cost or accumulation.
  • For this article I'll assume you already know the basics of RC, if not I really recommend the interactive tutorial from jason.today or the article from MAX Here is a quick recap as well.
  • Industry observers note that the main point of RC is combining the samples/rays for our GI in a way that utilizes them most effectively.This results in a more correct output with less samples.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, radiance cascades is a technique that massively improves global illumination without much extra cost or accumulation. In this article I'll go over the recent technique of Ray Splitting which allows the use of RC (Radiance cascades)in 3D without huge costs, and how to implement it. Note that the code examples are modified for clearability, so might not fully work.

For this article I'll assume you already know the basics of RC, if not I really recommend the interactive tutorial from jason.today or the article from MAX Here is a quick recap as well.

Industry observers note that the main point of RC is combining the samples/rays for our GI in a way that utilizes them most effectively.This results in a more correct output with less samples. The way of combining this relies on the penumbra hypothesis. Which states that, when you are close to a light source you need fewer rays (less angular resolution) to find the light.

In addition when you are close to a light you need more probes (spatial resolution) to get correct shadows.

Sources indicate that to interpolate the half shadow, we need the light at both sides. Further away this spacing can be bigger to still get probes on both sides.

By merging layers ranging from (high resolution, low direction count) to (low resolution, high direction count) that correspond to an interval of the ray, we get best of both of these in the range that matters.

RC requires storing our light into a grid of probes. This becomes a problem in 3D due to the massive memory cost that introduces. since probe counts scale ^3.

Even if we would only put this around the camera it would cost way too much memory to get a decent resolution.Luckily we only need probes where we need light, which is on all visible surfaces.So we need a way to only put probes on visible geometry.

To only spawn probes on visible surfaces, we reconstruct world positions from the screen.We round these positions to a grid of cells.

According to recent reports, to store our light in these cells we need a buffer of probes. To allocate this we use a hashtable. Creating a hash for each cell allows us to promptly allocate a slot for each of these without much fighting between threads.We also store an AppendBuffer with a list of the probes we allocated, this will be used later to launch our next passes indirectly.(this somewhat goes against the use of the hashtable, but the table will be needed more later)We clear and fill this table every frame and with this we get a table of sparsely allocated probes.

We can visualize/debug our probes in a separate pass.

With this gather pass we now have a single cascade of probes allocated.However we need multiple cascades of lowering resolution to do RC. For this we need to fill separate hashtables for each cascade, we could just re-run our shader for each cascade but that would be very innefficient. We already have our highest detail probes and there are significantly less of them than we have pixels. So instead of running over all pixels again, we can just go over all the probes we just allocated, for each of these we just halve their position to get the cascade above it. Any duplicates we get from this are handled by the hashtable.We run this bottom up for all cascades. The number of cascades we need is somewhat arbitrairy based on your scene size i'll be using 4.

Note that when visualizing your higher cascades you need to shift your positions when creating the key.

Normally to get the lighting at every probe, we shoot a set amount of rays into random directions from each probe.This however comes with quite a few challenges.Ray counts become very significant with good enough spatial and angular resolution. But the main problem is probe positioning, since our probes are in a grid they are not aligned with the surfaces which can cause a bunch of rays to shoot below the surface. This can cause overocclusion and light leaking, and also makes it so we cannot shoot rays in just a hemisphere.

The 2 red rays in this probe here got unfairly blocked because the probe is too far into the ground.

This would cause dark splotches in our lighting.So instead we can trace the rays from reconstructed world positions and put these into the probes that are at that spot.This way rays are sent from real geometry avoiding this problem.

Here the blue rays are sent from the position gotten from the screen, then moved into the closest probe.

Sources indicate that however, in RC each cascade does not contain the full ray, only a interval/segment of it. Sending multiple rays for each interval at each pixel would be quite inefficient. Instead we do it the other way around, we trace the full ray and pick the interval (and thus cascade) that it would have hit in based on its hit distance. We fill the hit interval's cascade with the lighting, and then mark transparancy / that a ray traveled through them in the cascades below the hit one.

The red ray hit inside the second cascade, and thus is binned into the second and first cascade.

Sources indicate that we store this in multiple bins per probe, one for each direction. We need to lay out these directions evenly and most importantly in a way that scales so that our merging evenly combines them into lower cascades. For shooting each ray we can just pick a random direction in a hemisphere at our hit.

With this we should now have every cascade filled with its interval of light.If we display this by just averaging all bins in an output pass, we can see the rings of light this contains.

We now want to merge these intervals together so we can get our entire path of light. We do this by going through our cascades from top down. We need to interpolate the directions and probes. Starting with directions, since our directions are evenly mapped to 4 times more in the above cascade we evenly interpolate these in our own cascade.

Industry observers note that however we need to also keep in account the transparency in this merging. If a ray was already blocked in the direction we're merging in the lower cascade/interval we shouldn't merge it downwards.

Here the middle interval is blocked, so we should not merge the light from the last interval, or it will leak in front of the wall.

Sources indicate that this merges our directions from the closest probe. Instead we want to check all the above probes and blend between them.For this we need to keep in mind probe spacing, each lower cascade has 8 probes inside 1 upper probe. So we shouldnt evenly blend.

According to recent reports, it's also notable to keep in mind that our grid is sparse, meaning the 8 surrounding probes will probably not all be there. This can be resolved by only weighing and sampling the probes that actually exist. Additionally, not all our probes are of the same quality. The amount of rays a probe contains and thus how accurate it is, is based on its visibility on the screen. We should also adjust for this, giving a higher weight to probes that contain more rays.

Recent findings suggest that with this we now have our full ray inside of the lowest cascade. To display this in our output shader, we have to merge the directions of the cascade into 1 value for each pixel, using the normal of the pixel to weigh the probes.

Right now we have a even grid of probes, which works fine for small scenes. But our probes get very small on the screen further away.This has 2 major problems. We shoot our rays from the screen, so the number of rays in a probe is based on how many pixels it occupies on the screen. So very small probes only get one ray or maybe even less.Secondly, the number of probes we spawn explodes further away which costs a lot of memory and is expensive to merge.By adding a form of LODs to our probes we solve both these problems, at only the cost of lower resolution lighting far away.This is very similar to cascaded shadow maps which makes naming confusing and thus we call them LODs/Levels.For each higher LOD we also halve the resolution similarly to our higher cascades although we keep the direction count the same. To do this we just halve our cell position each level. However for this we need to add a level index to our per probe key. We need to do this since our halved positions can overlap with the lower level.We can just bitshift this index after the rest of our key.Since everything else uses the hashtable, this should automatically work with the rest of our code assuming we calculate the key in the same way.

Recent findings suggest that this fixes a lot of flickering or overallocation further away, however it creates significant seams where the LODs change.So we want to blend in between these seams. To do this we keep some probes of overlap, allocating probes of both levels and also binning the ray into both.Wherever we calculate our level we instead calculate the range, making sure to keep correct weights so we do not double the light at the seam.

This should result in smooth, although flickering results.

Recent findings suggest that due to the benefits of splitting & merging with RC our single frame result is already pretty good. But since we still send random rays, there is still some flickering especially in probes that did not get many rays. We can fix this by accumulating our probes over time. This doesnt come with the drawbacks of most temporal effects. Since our probes are spatially stable, there is no smearing from bad reprojection. And since there is not a lot of noise in after a single frame there is barely any ghosting. So the only drawback is slower lighting updates.

Example of smearing using Lumen.

No smearing or much ghosting with RC.

Industry observers note that currently we clear and allocate the hashtable every frame, so our probe index moves every frame. To temporally accumulate we want our probes to keep the same index, so that we keep the old frame's result in their spot in the buffer. One way of doing this is by adding a layer of indirection to our hashtable, instead of storing the index into our data buffer in the table we store an index into another list of indices. That way we can add a pass that re-allocates our previous frame's results with the same index as the data. We also need to keep track of the lifetime of probes, to know which probes to reallocate or not, and resetting their lifetime if they are on screen.

Industry observers note that the hashtable should now be stable, you can test this using the debug output code from earlier, outputting the index. Probes shouldn't change color unless they go off the screen. With stable probes temporally accumulating is easy, when going over the probes (in the merge pass or in a separate pass) we just re-add the probes accumulated light and weights with a falloff. With that you should now have clean single bounce GI.

Recent findings suggest that currently light only bounces once from where we are looking. Things only start looking really good when we do multiple bounces. To achieve this we need to trace 1 extra bounce ray everywhere, from which we can get infinite bounces over time. To get one bounce, we just shoot an extra light ray from the hits of our primary ray. To do this we output our hit positions and normals in our ray generation shader, then run a second one from that spot.

The first hit is stored, then another random ray is sent from that hit position.

Recent findings suggest that this gives us a single real bounce, but increasing this to more would be very expensive. Instead we can sample the probes to apply GI to this, with the temporal accumulation that gives us an extra bounce every frame. However since our probes are only allocated where we are looking, we wouldn't be able to get this bounce light from outside of the screen, since there are no probes to sample from. To resolve this we allocate a separate secondary probe cache for this, we allocate extra probes at the hit positions of our primary ray. We fill these with radiance from the bounce ray, in the same way as our primary ray. To accumulate this to multiple bounces, we sample this cache at the hits of our primary and secondary rays.

Industry observers note that in one frame we send the primary ray, which allocates a probe filled with the bounce ray. The next frame a different bounce ray hits the same secondary probe. Since it samples the cache it then also contains the previous bounce. Over frames this stacks to infinite bounces.

In a recent development, this gives us infinite bounces, however it is limited to only the area covered by the single bounce ray, since that one allocates the secondary probes.We can re-use almost our whole system for this secondary probe. We already have LODs over distance, by allocating the secondary probes at at least 2 LODs higher it can fit into the same hashtable/probes without conflicts. If we also add these to the active probes the merge pass will merge their cascades as well. With that we get nice looking multi bounce GI.

According to recent reports, for simplicity I kept out a lot of optimizations or better ways to do things. I won't go over how to fully optimize but will briefly go over the main improvements that can be done to get this running well.

One major improvement in quality is choosing directions in a better way, currently we choose completely random directions.But there are multiple semi random sequences that accumulate to good results significantly quicker.By using a deposit count per probe as an index into something like the R2 sequence or blue noise, direction coverage accumulates significantly faster.

Apart from tracing, our merging & applying pass is the most expensive.It's sampling a lot of data across a low amount of threads.For example the bin merging can be done across threads, loading the 8 probes together and having each thread load a bin, merging them as a group.

Raytracing cost is by far the most expensive part.We can skip a percentage of pixels every frame to reduce cost significantly, although with the drawback of slower accumulation and thus more ghosting.Balancing this with probe sizes can improve the accumulation but at the cost of light resolution.This allows for a nice way of tweaking quality vs performance. It might also be worth replacing (some of) the rays with cheaper ones like screen space rays or sampling an sdf or voxel approximation of the world.

Almost all of the cost of this goes to actual tracing. For my implemention in Unreal on my 5070 Laptop GPU in San Miguel the cost of RC is about ~2ms depending on probe sizing.Although with ~13ms on top of raytracing at 2spp (1 primary 1 bounce) and another ~2ms for depositing the rays.The expensive tracing cost is very variable, depending on scene size and tracing performance in general.

The main points of error are light leaking in spots smaller than a (secondary) probe, and softer shadows. (presumably due to not enough base directions).

"Split Radiance Cascades: Real-Time Global Illumination via Sparse Radiance Probes": https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20384.

Jason Mcghee's article: https://jason.today/rc.

RC Wiki: https://radiance.wiki/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

According to recent reports, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In a recent development, in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

It has been revealed that in the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

Fast-Anything: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (391 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, don't rewrite it in Rust.
  • Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/.
  • fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow.

Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway.

fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible.

Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain (rustup).

Industry observers note that --agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use.

That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time.

Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from examples/.

Recent findings suggest that fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×.

According to recent reports, it ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, typed arrays…), including ones in your entry script when its main code sits under if __name__ == "__main__": (or if __FILE__ == $0). In Java and PHP that means static methods (and PHP functions), in Go plain functions, in C and C++ free functions and static methods. scan says why anything else can't move yet.

Ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C and C++ need no headers, bindings or extra tools: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly. Any language that can call C can use that bridge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The new terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:.

Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.

Industry observers note that several sellers who had run shops for years said they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.

In a recent development, kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.

James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.

Recent findings suggest that etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.

Industry observers note that he stated third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.

Some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.

Etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after users complained, the Times reported.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.
