Tech Report: Back pain mattress deals at Helix, Saatva, Plank and Brooklyn Bedding compared — what we recommend based on our testing

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, quality sleep and back pain do not go hand in hand, but a comfortable mattress that relieves discomfort can make a huge difference to how well you sleep at night.
  • Sources indicate that below, we've selected four beds that fit the specific criteria we recommend for high levels of comfort and support when you have back pain.
  • The Helix Midnight Luxe is the best mattress for side sleepers we've tested thanks to blissful pressure relief along the shoulders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, quality sleep and back pain do not go hand in hand, but a comfortable mattress that relieves discomfort can make a huge difference to how well you sleep at night. The best mattresses for back pain that we've tested are often specialist beds been engineered to support the spine and reduce lumbar pressure. But as our team of testers have discovered first hand, many of the best mattresses you can buy online also boast excellent lumbar support.

Sources indicate that below, we've selected four beds that fit the specific criteria we recommend for high levels of comfort and support when you have back pain. Even better, there are excellent Black Friday mattress deals on each of them. Let's take a look...

The Helix Midnight Luxe is the best mattress for side sleepers we've tested thanks to blissful pressure relief along the shoulders. Zoned lumbar support and ACA accreditation makes it a top choice for back pain, too. There's 25% off the Luxe in the Helix mattress sale, taking a queen to $1,874 (was $2,498.66), with a year's trial and lifetime warranty.

Our Helix Midnight Luxe review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½ (9,800+ reviews).

According to recent reports, the Rx is our top recommendation for anyone living with significant back or joint conditions, such as scoliosis or sciatica. The current Saatva Black Friday deal shaves a hefty $425 off all sizes of the RX with our semi-exclusive link, bringing queen down to $3,214 (was $3,639). It comes with a year's trial, lifetime warranty, and free white glove delivery.

Our Saatva Rx review score: ★★★★½User score: ★★★★★ (600+ reviews).

A 30% off Brooklyn Bedding mattress sale brings a queen CopperFlex Essential down to $489.30 (was $699), which is excellent value for money on a bed that hits the right notes for back support. We found it to be a good choice for side and lighter weight back sleepers, but too plush for stomach sleepers. It also comes with a year's sleep trial and limited lifetime warranty.

Our Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential review score: ★★★½User score: ★★★★½ (800+ reviews).

It has been revealed that this double-sided ultra-firm mattress offers a reassuringly sturdy sleep surface, delivering exceptional top-to-toe support. The current 30% off Black Friday deal is the biggest discount we've tracked on the Plank, bringing a queen down to $1,025.50 (was $1,465). Like the Luxe and the Rx above, it comes with ACA accreditation, plus a year's sleep trial, limited lifetime warranty and fast shipping.

Our Plank Firm review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½.

For a mattress to be considered a good option for anyone with back pain, it needs to perform well in three specific areas; pressure relief, temperature regulation, and edge support.

Sources indicate that in order to select only the beds that offer meaningful relief to people with a bad back, we've combed our test data to ensure each of the mattresses featured here have scored a minimum of 3.5 out of 5 in our pressure relief, temperature and edge support tests. Here's how the Helix Midnight Luxe, Saatva Rx, Plank Firm and Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential performed and compare across these crucial metrics:.

Pressure relief score (out of 5).

According to recent reports, temperature regulation: Reliable temperature regulation is an notable feature of a mattress for back pain. Waking up hot and sweaty can lead to more movement (like kicking off the covers), which can cause further injury. Pressure relief: This is a term to describe how much cushioning there is along the touch points of the mattress. For example, for side sleepers, this will be your shoulders, hips and knees. For back sleepers, this will likely be your lumbar region and upper back and shoulders. Minimal pressure relief can lead to a build-up of pressure, which can exacerbate existing pain. Edge Support: This describes how sturdy a mattress is at its edges and corners. This is an important feature for any mattress, but especially those with back pain who may need to sit comfortably and safely before standing.

The Helix Midnight Luxe is superbly comfortable for side sleepers, and it's also an excellent choice for those with lower and upper back pain, as well as hip pain. As a luxury hotel-style hybrid, it is a premium mattress. However, a current 25% sale means you can buy a queen Midnight Luxe for $1,874 at Helix. The pillow top is crafted from high density foam which cushions the shoulders hips and knees, but also keeps the spine in healthy alignment while sleeping. This high density foam also works to gently cradle the lumbar region, which is the 'S' shape of your back. Underpinning this support are up to 1,000 individually wrapped coils that prevent the hips from sinking. Our lead tester, who has experienced recurrent lower back pain for the past decade, felt none of the pain she usually experiences while sleeping on the Luxe. Temperature wise, our test data mirrored our real life experience. It's a breathable bed with reliably sturdy edges for sitting on before standing.The Luxe is accredited by the American Chiropractic Association and is a great fit for aches and pains. However, those with more pronounced back pain have the option to upgrade to ErgoAlign. This is a layer of denser foam around the mid-section, bolstering support in this area. Luxe is a great option for side and back sleeper with back ache but for significant back pain, we recommend the Saatva Rx below.

The Saatva Rx is our top recommendation for those living with significant back or joint conditions, such as sciatica or arthritis. It's an ACA accredited specialist mattress, and it's priced accordingly (it's $3,214 for a queen at Saatva in this year's Saatva Black Friday sale). A large part of what sets the Rx apart from other back pain beds pain is its Therapeutic Support Core. This is made up of the brand’s proprietary Wave-Tech Foam and individually wrapped coils for support, cradling the spine in all sleep positions. Above that, a layer of micro-coils sandwiched between two slabs of high-density foam and a strip of gel-infused memory foam provides soothing support along the lumbar.Saatva rates the Rx as 'Supportive Plush' but our experience of sleeping on it was that it errs on the firmer side, making it a more comfortable choice for back and stomach sleepers. It's still comfy for side sleepers, but our lead tester — who has mild scoliosis — felt her spine was better supported when sleeping on her back. For general aches and pains, we recommend the (slightly cheaper) Saatva Classic Mattress instead, which does an excellent job of soothing mild back and hip pain.

It has been revealed that it's a common misconception that people with back pain need a solid mattress. However, some people simply prefer the feel of a firm bed. And at 30% off for Black Friday, a queen Plank Firm is $1,025.50 at Plank, which is excellent value for money on this top rated firm mattress.The Plank Firm is a dual-sided all foam mattress rated as Firm on one side and Extra Firm on the other. It's been crafted from the inside out, where 6" of high density foam underpins the unyielding sleep surface. Regardless of how you flip it, make no mistake, this is a firm mattress. With its 2" top layer of comfort foam which provides cushioning around the touch points of the bed, the Firm side will have wider appeal. However, with just 0.75" slither of comfort foam, the Extra Firm side feels reassuringly solid for those who want to keep their spine in healthy alignment when sleeping on their stomach.It's accredited by the ACA and boasts superb motion isolation, which is good news for bed sharers. It's also nice and sturdy around the edge. However, with a score of 3.5 out of 5 for temperature control, it just scrapes through our benchmark of being temperature regulating enough for it to be considered a good choice for back pain. For hot sleepers, we recommend upgrading to the GlacioTex cooling layer.

Industry observers note that in a mattress for back pain guide featuring ACA accredited beds with zoned lumbar support, you might be wondering why we have added the Essential to the mix, a mattress that at $489.30 for a queen at Brooklyn Bedding costs a fraction of the price and boasts none of those things.That's because, when combing our test data, it became apparent that the Essential performs well enough in crucial areas (temperature regulation, edge support and pressure relief) to make it a good choice for side sleepers looking for cushioning around their shoulders and hips, without sacrificing healthy spinal alignment. It's supportive enough for lighter weight back sleepers, but heavier bodies with need something sturdier to prevent their hips from sinking in this position. The Essential comes in 5 different heights ranging from 6"to 14" and we tested the 10". Increasing the height will likely mean increasing the support... and also the price. For a sturdier all foam mattress for back sleeping within a similar price range, we would opt for the Siena Signature. It scored 3.3 out of 5 for temperature regulation but is a fantastic budget friendly, firmer choice. For ACA accreditation, enhanced cooling and zoned lumbar support, we recommend the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Pro Hybrid, a mid-range marvel coming in at under $1,000 for a queen in the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales.

Nicola is the Sleep Editor at Tom’s Guide. With a career in journalism spanning two decades, Nicola brings experience to the team and the knowledge of what makes a great article, whether that’s a how-to mattress cleaning feature, a deep dive into melatonin gummies, or an in-depth mattress review. As a sleep editor, few better understand how crucial a decent mattress is to the overall quality of our sleep, and precisely how our sleep impacts our physical and mental health. As well as tackling the vast topic of sleep, Nicola joins the raft of expert mattress specialists at Tom’s Guide, who test and compare a wide range of mattresses in order to guide readers towards the very best options on the market.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Industry observers note that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell notes. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

Industry observers note that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

According to recent reports, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team revealed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

It has been revealed that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga claims, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

It has been revealed that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga states. “It was just major enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

Industry observers note that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Sources indicate that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” notes Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson claims. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

In a recent development, nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Industry observers note that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga notes.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

According to recent reports, but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more crucial than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell claims. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” notes neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Recent findings suggest that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, indicates experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu notes.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” indicates neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

According to recent reports, “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

Industry observers note that if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Recent findings suggest that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell notes. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he claims. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

According to recent reports, the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How promptly are doctors picking up on this fresh technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference.

Industry observers note that SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares. It will hold an indirect stake of about 14.1%, it said in a filing on Friday.

Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing. The move puts SK Hynix ahead of Toshiba, Kioxia’s former parent, which held 10.46% in early November, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

Industry observers note that SPC2 is a special-purpose tech giant set up for the 2018 deal. SK Hynix will convert 129bn yen ($810m) of its bonds into 129,000 shares. It will also buy Bain Capital’s remaining 1,001 SPC2 shares for 100m yen. The steps close in December, leaving SK Hynix as SPC2’s sole owner.

Apart from the payment to Bain, the deal adds no fresh money, MoneyToday reported, citing the manufacturer. SK Hynix called it a follow-up step after it sold out of a separate Kioxia fund in June. Gains from that sale funded about 7tn won ($5.2bn) of special dividends in the third quarter.

SK Hynix joined the Bain-led group that bought Kioxia, then Toshiba Memory, in 2018. It put in 395bn yen at the time.

In a recent development, both companies make NAND, the chips used for storage in phones and AI servers. SK Hynix held 19% of the global NAND market in the second quarter and Kioxia 14%, according to Counterpoint figures cited by Bloomberg. Together that tops market leader Samsung’s 28%.

According to recent reports, the 2018 deal caps SK Hynix at 15% of Kioxia’s voting shares until 2028, unless Kioxia agrees otherwise. Kioxia lists the stake as a risk factor in its annual report, citing a possible conflict of interest, Bloomberg reported.

Both sides say nothing changes in how Kioxia is run. A Kioxia spokesperson mentioned its management will stay independent.

According to recent reports, “We right now have no plans to further buy or sell shares in Kioxia. We will continue to respect Kioxia’s independent management going forward,” an SK Hynix official noted.

Masahiro Wakasugi of Bloomberg Intelligence sees little change in the short run.

The move is “unlikely to materially change near-term NAND competition,” Wakasugi wrote.

Industry observers note that the stake still gives SK Hynix some say over significant decisions, he added. That includes the power to oppose a possible deal between Kioxia and Sandisk.

According to recent reports, separately, SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a buyout of SK Hynix itself. The Korean firm reported a 632% profit jump in October, even as memory stocks slid.

Apple is expected to release the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 sometime next spring. Ahead of that launch, fresh dummy units posted to social media today give us a closer look at the devices, including a major update to the iPhone Air 2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Sources indicate that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Sources indicate that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#96883. The Mythology of Conscious AI
