Reversing the Next-Page Prefetcher in Skylake-X

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intel publishes very little about next-page prefetchers in their P-cores.
  • In a recent development, hardware prefetch enhancement: A next-page prefetcher (NPP) is added in Intel microarchitecture code name Ivy Bridge.
  • A recent glitch of the optimization manual states that Redwood Cove includes a Last Level Cache (LLC) Page Prefetcher which is like NPP but with a slightly more sophisticated prefetch algorithm:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel publishes very little about next-page prefetchers in their P-cores. Back in the Ivy Bridge days, it was known that IVB included a next-page prefetcher thanks to this ancient excerpt from an old copy of the Intel Architectures Optimization Reference Manual:.

In a recent development, hardware prefetch enhancement: A next-page prefetcher (NPP) is added in Intel microarchitecture code name Ivy Bridge. The NPP is triggered by sequential accesses to cache lines approaching the page boundary, either upwards or downwards.

A recent glitch of the optimization manual states that Redwood Cove includes a Last Level Cache (LLC) Page Prefetcher which is like NPP but with a slightly more sophisticated prefetch algorithm:.

In a recent development, the LLC Page Prefetcher extends the Next-Page-Prefetcher algorithm, which detects a sequence of accesses that are about to reach the end of a page (either going up towards the next page in memory or down towards the previous page in memory) and triggers a linear prefetch to the start of the next predicted page. NPP intends to prefetch the translation of the next page and initiate prefetching of the first few cache lines from that predicted page. The LLC Page Prefetch enhances Next-Page Prefetcher in two significant ways:.

According to recent reports, redwood Cove is a relatively recent microarchitecture which shipped in Meteor Lake P-cores starting late 2023. Ivy Bridge on the other hand is very old; It launched back in 2012 and was discontinued by 2015 right before Skylake launched. That raises the question, what happened in-between? Did every microarchitecture after IVB include a next-page prefetcher?

In a recent development, it’s unlikely that the details remain unchanged from one microarchitecture to the next but as it turns out, I recently got unlimited access to a Skylake-X machine that I didn’t have to pay a single dime for. Given the setup, it’s only natural I got nerd-sniped into reversing the next-page prefetcher…and that’s what this post is about. I hope you enjoy it!

Recent findings suggest that hardware component that preloads data that the program might need soon. The goal is to eliminate memory stalls when the CPU actually demands the piece of data that the prefetcher could have loaded earlier. All kinds of prefetchers exist in modern CPUs. Next-Line prefetchers prefetch the immediate next cache line when the N’th cache line is accessed. Stride prefetchers (usually IP-based) track the stride of consecutive memory accesses that originate from the same instruction and if the access pattern turns out to be regular enough, it eagerly initiates the load from address that it predicted. Next-Page Prefetchers preload page table entries into the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) provided software traverses memory pages in predictable manner. These by no means are the only three kind; a high-performance CPU may implement many other types of prefetchers, some of which are documented in this Intel whitepaper.

In a recent development, prefetchers that are required to act fast are logically simple and tend not to cross page boundaries because that may complicate things with, e.g. page faults and page walks on TLB misses. For example, the next-line prefetcher is supposed to fetch the next cache line if the accesses are sequential, but if the next cache line sits in a different page it may decide not to prefetch at all. Next-page prefetchers are slightly different in that regard; they prefetch the next page table entry (PTE) into the TLB. They have to work across page boundaries by design.

In this post I’ll try to answer the following questions:.

But before we start, let’s prepare the stage for our experiments.

If you don’t intend to run the experiments described in this post, you can skip this part.

Recent findings suggest that documenting the many details of performance monitoring on various platforms deserves a post of its own, and a fairly long one at that. For simplicity I’m only going to focus on Linux. Linux allows configuring performance monitoring events via the perf_event_open syscall. That’s what I’ll be using in my experiments too but generally speaking, you don’t need special system APIs to access PMU counters. At least on Intel, you only need some way of writing a set of performance monitoring MSRs (usually only the IA32_PERFEVTSELx MSRs) and read the counters back from a set of corresponding IA32_PMCx MSRs. WRMSR and RDMSR require Ring0 access so if you’re on Windows, you’d have to write a kernel-mode driver and use __readmsr/__writemsr intrinsics to read/write the relevant MSRs. That said, the hard part of making custom drivers for Windows isn’t writing the driver itself, rather convincing the kernel to load your driver. More on that in a future blog post.

In a recent development, performance monitoring tools that allow reading PMU counters (e.g. perf, VTune) may also work. I’d stick to perf_event_open because it allows better control over the exact segment of code I need to measure. The manpage includes an example of how to use perf_event_open. For our experiments we need three things in order:.

We’ll write a helper for each of these steps: configure_event_group to configure the events, start_counters to enable the counters, and stop_counters to stop and read the counters. With that aside, here’s configure_event_group:.

Full source code of every experiment, data structure, and helpers used in this article can be found on github. The group_fd identifies the event group that you configure via perf_event_open. You can use that group_fd to perform certain operations on the event group, like enabling or disabling the counters. That’s what we’re going to do next: enable the counters with start_counters which is defined like this:.

According to recent reports, calling start_counters sets off the counters for every event configured in the event group identified by group_fd. At this point we’ll run our workload, then call stop_counters to stop and read the counters:.

Recent findings suggest that before we can read PMU counters using the functions defined above, we need to tweak some settings on Linux. Depending on your distro, certain restrictions may apply by default on hardware PMU access due to security reasons. You can overcome them by setting perf_event_paranoid to 0 or -1:.

You may also need to disable THP and pin the calling thread to a core if there’s too much going on in your machine.

According to recent reports, now we have all the pieces required to start monitoring hardware events. Throughout this post we’d work with the following events:.

It’s note hard to observe that the event configs are of the form 0x, where Umask and EventSel are coming straight from the “PROGRAMMING INFO” column of the corresponding event in the perfmon website (the ‘H’ suffix is Intel’s way of saying the number is given in hexadecimal). Not all event configs are derived this way, but it’s enough for the simple ones we’re gonna use here.

Industry observers note that SKX (codename for Skylake-X) has two TLB levels: L1 and L2. Each SKX core gets a physically separate L1 data TLB (dTLB) and L1 instruction TLB (iTLB). The L2 TLB (also called Second Level TLB or STLB) is unified, i.e. both instruction and data PTEs go to the same STLB.

Recent findings suggest that both L1 and L2 TLBs are partitioned based on the page size. L1 dTLB has a total of 100 entries: 64 reserved for 4k pages, 32 for 2M or 4M pages, and 4 for 1G pages. The dTLB is 4-way set associative so each set can hold 4 page-table entries. The iTLB is also partitioned: has 128 entries for 4k pages, 16 entries for 2M or 4M pages, and none for 1G pages. The STLB has 1536 entries shared between 4k and 2M pages and an additional 16 entries for 1G huge pages. STLB is not inclusive of the L1 TLBs. That means at any given instance, a page-table entry may exist in one of the L1 TLBs, the STLB, or both.

Industry observers note that for the purposes of this post, we don’t need to dig any further into the geometry of SKX TLBs. It’s time to run some experiments!

The very first question that we should ask is whether the next-page prefetcher exists in SKX at all. NPPs seem like a good idea in general; given that Intel had the silicon budget to include one in Ivy Bridge, we expect the answer to be “Yes” in SKX too. To test this, we’ll design a workload that walks a mapped range of 1000 4K pages sequentially and measure how many TLB misses we get. I cannot imagine a more favourable access pattern for the NPP to kick in if it truly exists. If the workload below doesn’t trigger the prefetcher, we can safely conclude that SKX doesn’t have one.

In a recent development, not much going on here. We have a function that touches every byte in the mapped range starting at MAP_BASE. The seemingly useless zero helps ensure that loads from the mapped range execute serially. Take a closer look at how we’re using zero in the loop. Loading the next byte from the mapped range at iteration i depends on the value of zero computed at iteration i-1. Computing zero at iteration i-1 in turn depends on computing dummy at iteration i-1. We have a cyclic loop-carried dependency chain here: the load in map_base[i + zero] feeds add in dummy += .... The result of that add then feeds the and in zero = zero & .... Result of the and feeds the next load at iteration i+1. In layman terms, the loads at iteration i and iteration i+1 cannot execute together or out-of-order. This is intentional: alloweing out-of-order execution of the two loads could significantly perturb our results. We’ll see why in a moment.

The last line is a common trick to avoid the compiler throw away our computation; it’s falsely advertising that the inline asm uses the value of dummy computed in the loop and forcing the compiler to materialize dummy into a register.

With g++ -O2, the loop compiles to:.

Sources indicate that nice. A few instructions here and there but we got the loop compiled exactly how we wanted. Note that the dependency chain we just discussed translates exactly to assembly too. Running the workload gives the following count for the two events:.

Over a few runs DTLB_LOAD_MISSES.STLB_HIT fluctuates between the 50..75 band, but never exceeds 75. That’s already interesting: we walked through 1000 pages in the loop but DTLB_LOAD_MISSES.STLB_HIT is nowhere near 1000. DTLB_LOAD_MISSES.STLB_HIT = 70 means only 70 out of the 1000 PTE requests missed in dTLB and hit STLB. The obvious next question is what happened to rest of the 1000 - 70 = 930 fresh PTE requests that the loop might have initiated? There are two possible answers:.

It has been revealed that we can quickly rule out (1) because MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_LOADS = 1. So that leaves us with (2): about 930 latest PTE requests hit in the dTLB when the demand arrived. But that must mean that SKX has a prefetcher that’s prefilling the dTLB with future PTEs. Yep! It’s the next-page prefetcher in action. Well, strictly speaking this could also be a non-NPP prefetcher that is allowed prefetch beyond page boundaries but as they say, if it quacks like a duck, it’s the next-page prefetcher!

In a recent development, subtle point that is easy to miss: the prefetcher is loading entries into th dTLB. This doesn’t automatically prove or disprove that it’s also prefilling STLB. Perhaps a carefully designed experiment can unveil that secret, but that’s not my focus in this post. We’d also not worry about the iTLB for now.

Sources indicate that microarchitecture explorations typically require careful use of statistics to extract signal buried in noise. Luckily in this case the signal is so strong that we can get away with sloppiness.

Alright, we have established that SKX has a next-page prefetcher that prefills the dTLB. On to the next question!

Something in the loop in touch_all_bytes must have triggered the next-page prefetch. The most obvious guess is a load from the previous page. Question is, which load? Is it just a single load from a special offset? A set of loads? There are so many questions that could be asked here…we need an experiment that narrows down the space of possibilities. We can imagine a workload that touches only the left half of each page (bytes in the range page[0..2047], inclusive) and count the TLB misses. If we still see TLB miss numbers like in our first experiment, that’d mean accesses from the left half of the page triggers the prefetch. If we instead see TLB misses that add up to 1000 (or more), we can repeat the same experiment but this time touching the right half of the page (bytes in the range page[2048..4095], inclusive). A generic workload that accepts an offset and a slice_length can handle both cases:.

When touch_page_slice is called with offset = 0, slice_length = 2048, it walks left half of each of the 1000 mapped pages. Walking the right half is just as simple, just call touch_page_slice with offset = 2048 and slice_length = 2048. Results from walking the left half:.

Walking the left half generated MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_LOADS = 1001. That’s suspiciously close to the total number of pages we walked! The most sensible explanation is that the NPP did not trigger while walking the left half, thus every latest PTE request missed in the dTLB. Those misses then made it to STLB and then missed there too.

Alright, what about the right half? Here’s the result from waking the right half:.

It has been revealed that comparatively, walking the right half is not bad at all. In fact this time the prefetcher clearly did trigger. We can keep splitting the slice that triggers prefetch binary-search style and further narrow the access range. The table below demonstrates the results:.

According to recent reports, hmm, neither left nor right slice of the last row triggers the prefetcher. But we do know that walking page[3328..3455] does work. So here’s the upcoming strategy: we start our walk at offset 3328 but not stop at 3391, rather keep pushing the right edge one byte at a time until we cause the prefetcher to trigger. For example, we’d walk page[3328..3392] and if that didn’t trigger NPP, we’d walk page[3328..3393] and so forth. We expect that the prefetcher would trigger before we reach page[3328..3455]. We can reuse touch_page_slice here too; just call it with offset = 3328 and slice_length = 65,66,....

According to recent reports, it doesn’t take long to identify the slice that triggers prefetch: the sneaky page[3328..3392]. Calling touch_page_slice with offset = 3328 and slice_length = 65 immediately triggers the prefetch. If you’re into this kind of shannonigans, it shouldn’t take too long to notice that 3392 is the first byte into the 53rd cache line (counting zero-indexed) within a page. Ok, does that mean accessing the 53rd cache line triggers the prefetch? But that can’t be true because we accessed every single byte in the 53rd line and verified no prefetches (see “Right half” of the last row in the table). Moreover, offset 3328 starts the 52nd cache line (counting zero-indexed) within a page, so we also know that accessing every byte in the 52nd cache line also doesn’t trigger the prefetch (see the “Left half” of the last row in the table). Could it be that for the prefetcher to trigger, subsequent loads must cross the 52nd cache line into the 53rd cache line? If the prefetch condition truly is as simple as “two subsequent loads, one from cache line 52, the next from cache line 53”, then the following must hold:.

Sources indicate that to test these hypotheses, we need a workload that touches every byte in a page except a few. This should work:.

The strange looking trick to compute idx in the inner loop helps avoid a branch in the probe path. Yeah, we are also banking on the fact that the branch predictor would do just fine when we’re done walking a page in the inner loop and jump back to the outer loop. Strictly speaking, a branch mispredict shouldn’t mess with TLBs in a way that affects our results but in general, eliminating noise sources to the best of your ability is a good idea with these kind of experiments. Aside from that there’s not much going on here. We are skipping the range page[hole_offset, hole_offset+hole_length] and touching every other byte in the page. When i falls within the skipped range, we simply redirect the load to hole_offset - 1.

Industry observers note that ok so what are the results if we skip cache line 52 and 53, i.e. range page[3328, 3391] and page[3392, 3456]:.

Recent findings suggest that MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_LOADS = 1000 for both cases. This verifies (1) and (2) from our list of hypotheses. We can test (3) by calling touch_page_slice with offset = 3391 and slice_length = 2. Here are the results:.

As expected, merely touching a single byte in each of 52nd and 53rd cache lines engages the prefetcher. Now admittedly the experiment doesn’t prove the “any byte in either cache line” part; we’ve only shown that loading last byte in cache line 52 followed by the load of first byte in cache line 53 triggers the prefetch, but you can easily verify that by tweaking the parameters of touch_page_with_hole. For example, hole_offset = 3329 and hole_length = 126 touches first byte of line 52 and last byte of line 53, skipping everything in-between. This still triggers prefetch. To limit the size of this post, I’ll leave out certain details like that from here on after. I’d be happy to fill those gaps in the comment section if you have questions.

In a recent development, note that for the prefetcher to trigger, load from 52nd cache line must execute before the load from 53rd cache line (unless the prefetcher is bidirectional, but we’ll get to that in a minute). This is why it was crucial to introduce the dependency chain that throttles out-of-order execution of loads from the page.

In a recent development, if you’re wondering why would Intel design the prefetcher with such a thin trigger condition, you’re not alone. I had the same exact question. I mean, triggering prefetch when loads get closer and closer to the next page makes sense. But why put all your bets on crossing just the 52nd cache line?! It’d make more sense if any couple of accesses beyond a threshold triggered the prefetch. Peter Cordes (yeah, that Peter Cordes) had a brilliant answer on why this makes sense. Go read it if you’re interested.

It has been revealed that good question. Our experiments so far have only used loads. A sane person would think stores shouldn’t behave any different. But to my surprise, stores don’t seem to trigger prefetches at all. If you’re browsing the full source on GitHub you’d notice that we are faulting the mapped range with loads. That choice is deliberate: we’re intentionally mapping every virtual page in the mapped range to the physical zero page. This reduces cache footprint, and potentially restricts one more source of noise.

Recent findings suggest that we cannot keep doing this for this next experiment, though: we don’t want page faults in the probe path. So we switch to faulting with stores before we start the experiment. That out of the way, here’s the kernel we’ll use to verify no prefetch on stores:.

According to recent reports, running this produces MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_STORES = 1000. Note that this time we are measuring STLB misses on stores. You can verify that each of these misses start at least one page-walk by counting DTLB_STORE_MISSES.WALK_COMPLETED along with MEM_INST_RETIRED.STLB_MISS_STORES. That rules out the possibility of dTLB hits and a last-level TLB (other than STLB) catching all the misses from STLB.

Sources indicate that we have established that the next-page prefetcher prefetches at least one future PTE. We shouldn’t expect it to load more than one page ahead; it’s called next-page prefetcher for a reason. But let’s verify that with this simple experiment:.

The idea is to “heat up” the prefetcher by crossing 52nd cache line in the first poke_limit pages — that’s what the first loop does — then load first byte of future_limit pages beyond poke_limit in the second loop. We’ll call this function repeatedly, each time increasing future_limit by 1, and count the TLB misses. We can get a baseline with future_limit = 0 first:.

According to recent reports, over many runs, STLB miss baseline fluctuates between 1 and 3 but never seems to exceed 3. Alright, we can work with that. Now let’s try future_limit = 1:.

In a recent development, yep, expected! The last load in the “heater” must’ve triggered the prefetch for page at poke_limit, so future_limit = 1 shouldn’t increase the number of observed misses. What about future_limit = 2?

Looks like the NPP prefetches only one page ahead. If you gradually increase future_limit to 2, 3, 4…and beyond, you’d notice that number of STLB misses increase in roughly the same cadence. That’s a strong hint NPP is indeed fetching only one page ahead.

It has been revealed that does the prefetcher work backwards too? This is the last piece of the puzzle and fortunately very easy to test: just walk the mapped range backwards. If you get close to 1000 misses the answer is no, otherwise yes. Here’s the test:.

This is a bit shocking. If you recall from the “Introduction” section, Intel manuals seem to suggest the next-page prefetcher triggers while walking “upwards” (what I call forward) or “downward” (what I call backward). This behavior is documented for both Ivy Bridge and Redwood Cove, but that’s not what we see for SKX. I don’t have any theories explaining this disconnect between SKX and the other uarchs. If you do, feel free to share in the comments.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a software developer looking for a cool new way of optimizing program performance, probably nowhere. Optimizing programs for a single microarchitecture from a single CPU vendor is almost always a bad idea for anything with half-life beyond next Friday. My goal here is to share how I attempt reversing undocumented machine behavior and invite fellow nerds to kick-start discussions that hopefully help me or somebody else learn something new.

Sources indicate that that noted, if you’re one of those weirdos who can afford to care only about one type of machine (Skylake-X to be precise), you may find the details interesting from a practical PoV. Hardware security researchers may also find this stuff interesting; a large chunk of what I know about CPU microarchitectures is thanks to security folks obsessing over tiniest details of some hardware component, then use it as a data leak channel and write very elaborate papers detailing how their exploit works. Either way, I’m tired. This is too much writing for a first post. 👋.

Breaking: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • In a recent development, data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

In a recent development, data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

Sources indicate that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” claims Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Recent findings suggest that optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The firm’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

Recent findings suggest that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” notes Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Newly introduced Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

According to recent reports, inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

In a recent development, VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon claims this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How major do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also notable to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Sources indicate that taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr claims.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

It has been revealed that the startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” indicates Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

In a recent development, the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen indicates, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

In a recent development, both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr indicates. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

It has been revealed that free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another massive advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

Recent findings suggest that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

According to recent reports, one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the firm unveiled a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch notes, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

It has been revealed that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch notes.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” indicates Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the organization’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

It has been revealed that lightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

Sources indicate that lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

Industry observers note that lightSolver’s team is presently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi states. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick Fresh, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

It has been revealed that the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Upcoming claims. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis.

Recent findings suggest that instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

It has been revealed that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Latest notes that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

Recent findings suggest that how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he claims. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Indicates Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

In a recent development, whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” notes Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

Tech Report: Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the tech giant’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Sources indicate that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

Industry observers note that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

In a recent development, I’m a significant fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”.

It has been revealed that apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

It has been revealed that another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

According to recent reports, it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

In a recent development, once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech owners may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

It has been revealed that is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026.

Palmer Luckey says the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it. Starshield is the Pentagon’s military satellite network, and SpaceX helps run it. The Anduril founder made the case to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey mentioned.

He was defending Elon Musk, who spoke later that day and accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. Luckey stated he likes Musk personally, so people should take his view “with a pound of salt”.

In a recent development, his argument ran like this. Russia has hinted that it could destroy the civilian Starlink network if Ukraine keeps using it for attacks. The same satellites that cover Ukraine also orbit over the US. So Musk should not have to risk his whole network when Washington will not risk its own, Luckey stated.

In a recent development, “Nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win. They just want them to not lose for as long as possible, which is a bizarre and absurd warfighting position,” he said.

It has been revealed that luckey said he fully supports Ukraine, and that Anduril has worked there since the second day of the war. Who America sells weapons to is not his call, he added.

“I’m a dog on a chain and I need to be kept that way,” Luckey said.

Luckey co-leads Project Meridian, the Pentagon’s 120-day study of future war, with Musk and Newt Gingrich. He said it looks at what war could look like in 2050, and that the MITRE Corporation runs it. The group met at Cheyenne Mountain the day before. It agreed to focus on ideas that have no champion in the Pentagon.

Sources indicate that one example is weather control, he stated, such as changing where rain falls at sea so forces get a clearer view of targets. He also took credit for pushing the Trump administration to rename the Defense Department the Department of War.

Sorkin read him a criticism from Wes Bryant, who until last year ran the Pentagon’s assessment of civilian harm. Bryant called Meridian a sign of oligarchy in government. Luckey remarked more than 20 people sit on it, including retired generals and admirals. Nobody attacked Eric Schmidt for joining the Defense Innovation Board under Joe Biden, he said, and the report will be public.

“They were designed for the type of cell phone that Abraham Lincoln would have used,” he said.

“I am way more afraid of the civilian collateral side for dumb weapons than I am for smart weapons,” Luckey said.

In a recent development, “Executions should be brutal. They should be violent,” he noted.

#96869. My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tymscar ↗ Open Full Page

My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tymscar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet.
  • Sources indicate that my ISP is pretty cool.
  • I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

Sources indicate that my ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦.

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

It has been revealed that I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

Industry observers note that so it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast….

Sources indicate that I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

It has been revealed that well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:.

Sources indicate that so basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Sources indicate that here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

Sources indicate that I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

It has been revealed that the problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the concerns don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1….

According to recent reports, so I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:.

According to recent reports, why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:.

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

I think the massive takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

FT, NYT tie Alice Huang’s chip network to gaming tycoons and PLA suppliers

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.
  • Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday.
  • TNW has not independently verified either report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s headquarters on San Tomas Expressway in Santa Clara, California.

Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, had links to gaming tycoons, hundreds of shell companies and an alleged Cambodian criminal group, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Together they formed a network that supplied Nvidia chips to China. A day earlier, The Newly introduced York Times tied companies linked to her family to suppliers of China’s military.

TNW has not independently verified either report. US officials suspect Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, the Times first reported in October, describing a Chinese spy plot. Beijing calls the claim a smear. Jensen Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive on 12 November after admitting an affair with her. They are not related.

The FT’s Zijing Wu and Haohsiang Ko traced the Alice Huang chip network through hundreds of filings and more than a dozen sources. Its companies made billions moving Nvidia chips into China, not necessarily aware of the full picture, the paper reported.

It has been revealed that it started with Inspur, one of Nvidia’s largest server partners in China. The US put Inspur on its entity list in March 2023, but not its part-owned US unit. Renamed Aivres, that unit kept trading with Nvidia. Inside Nvidia there were questions over whether it should count as a partner, a person with direct knowledge told the FT. Nvidia concluded that it met all compliance and export control rules.

Some of Inspur’s Chinese clients then turned to Century Huatong, an online gaming group turned data centre investor. The answer, people familiar with the blueprint noted, was an offshore shell branded as a “neocloud”. That shell became Megaspeed, with Huang as its trusted public face.

Kang Wei, whom the FT calls her husband and the Times her business partner, was an early investor in Century Huatong, filings show. Megaspeed grew out of the Singapore arm of 7Road, a gaming firm that Huang and Century Huatong both backed. Its Malaysian unit, Speedmatrix, declared about $4.6bn of imports from Aivres in the year to December 2025. The FT cites ImportGenius trade data.

Industry observers note that the last step was smuggling the chips into China. Hu Xiaowei filled at least part of that role, people familiar with the matter told the FT. US authorities call Hu the “second-in-command” at Prince Group. The US Treasury has named the group a transnational criminal organisation. Hu was arrested in Japan this summer.

According to recent reports, A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies noted Hu never worked for the business and called the US allegations unsupported. The FT could not reach Hu.

Nvidia said it put Megaspeed and a subsidiary on its block list in 2025 and has also restricted sales to Aivres. Megaspeed has said it runs a lawful business, and that Huang left in August 2025. Tencent, which owns 10.1% of Century Huatong, said it knew nothing of the activities. The FT found no evidence that Tencent or Alibaba took part.

According to recent reports, the Times reviewed a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an intelligence firm staffed by former intelligence officers. About $3.6bn of Chinese state money flowed through companies tied to Huang’s family or associates, it found. The money funded projects including data centres with Nvidia chips. The Times said it confirmed many of the ties itself.

According to recent reports, most links are indirect, the Times stated, and it is unclear whether the military used any of the computing power. The paper had already reported that Megaspeed’s backer Alibaba co-founded a military-linked lab.

“Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it,” Strider’s chief executive, Greg Levesque, told the Times.

It has been revealed that both papers point to Century Litong, a Shanghai firm founded by Century Longteng. The FT claims Longteng was a venture between Century Huatong and a vehicle Huang controlled with her sister. The Times names the sister’s firm.

According to recent reports, century Litong was a key distributor of smuggled Nvidia chips in China, people with knowledge of the deals told the FT. The Information first reported its role. Its owner, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, also controls a maker of Chinese radar and missile parts, the Times reported.

Sources indicate that nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to Century Litong’s Hong Kong unit, licence files released on Thursday by a House committee show. An Nvidia spokesman told the Times that, despite receiving some licences, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and had not and would not ship to that firm. Century Litong says it has no dealings with Huang. Nvidia’s shares, meanwhile, have had their worst run since 2008.

Is 'fork' missing operation in sandboxes?
